title: How to Plan for Retirement When You Still Have a Mortgage
description: Managing debt in the distribution phase.
content:
The old rule was 'Enter retirement debt-free.' Today, nearly 40% of retirees still have a mortgage. With home prices high and careers starting later, carrying a mortgage into retirement is the new normal. It is not necessarily a disaster, but it requires a different withdrawal strategy. You need a larger portfolio to generate the cash flow to service the debt. This guide explains the math of retiring with a mortgage and how to ensure it doesn't sink your plan.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Required Income' Spike: A $2,000 mortgage payment means you need an extra $24,000/year in income. Using the 4% rule, that means you need an extra $600,000 in your portfolio just to cover the house.
  • Interest Rate Arbitrage: If your mortgage is 3% and cash earns 5%, do not pay it off. Keep the cash. You earn the spread. If mortgage is 7%, pay it off aggressively.
  • Liquidity Risk: The danger of a mortgage is that it is a fixed cost. If the market crashes and you have to sell stocks to pay the mortgage, you lock in losses. You need a larger 'Cash Bucket'.
  • Tax Deductions: Mortgage interest might be deductible, but fewer retirees itemize now due to the higher Standard Deduction. Don't count on the tax break.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security cannot be garnished for credit card debt, but if you default on a mortgage, you lose the house. Housing is the one liability you must secure at all costs in retirement.

Pay Off vs. Invest

Scenario: You have $200,000 remaining on a mortgage at 4%. You have $200,000 cash.

Option A: Pay It Off

Pros: Monthly expenses drop by $1,500. You sleep better. Required portfolio size drops.
Cons: You lose $200k of liquidity. If you have a medical emergency, you can't get the money back out easily.

Option B: Keep the Mortgage

Pros: You keep $200k in the bank. It earns 5% ($10k/yr), which helps pay the 4% interest ($8k/yr). You have access to cash.
Cons: You have a monthly obligation. If interest rates on savings drop to 1%, the math turns against you.

The Verdict: If the rate is low (<4%), keep it. If high (>6%), pay it.

Safety Strategies

  1. The 5-Year Cash Reserve: If you keep the mortgage, you must keep 5 years of payments in safe assets (Cash/Bonds). This ensures you never have to sell stocks in a downturn to pay the bank.
  2. Recasting: If you can't pay it off fully, make a lump sum payment and 'Recast' the loan. This lowers the monthly payment while keeping the rate and term. It improves cash flow.
  3. Downsizing as Plan B: If the mortgage becomes a burden, be willing to sell. Don't hold onto the 'Family Home' if it makes you house poor. Equity is useless if you can't buy food.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I refinance in retirement?

It is harder. Banks look at income. If you don't have a salary, you have to prove income via asset depletion. It is easier to refinance before you quit your job.

What if I'm underwater?

You cannot retire. If you owe more than the house is worth, you are insolvent. You must keep working until the debt is cleared or the market recovers.

Is a Reverse Mortgage the answer?

It eliminates the monthly payment (you still pay tax/insurance), but the balance grows over time. It solves cash flow but eats equity. Use cautiously.
